Chapter 2: The Limits of Reform and the Persistence of Inequality
Picture this: a group of workers, gathered in a dimly lit meeting hall after a long, exhausting shift. You can almost see their tired faces, but in their eyes—there’s determination. They’re sharing stories, talking about hard-fought wins. Maybe it’s a shorter workday, or a safer piece of equipment. Every little improvement feels like a victory, proof of what they can accomplish together.
But as the night goes on, you can sense a quiet unease. For every step forward, there’s another step back. Wages go up, but then so do prices. Laws change, but suddenly, new loopholes appear. Progress is real, but so is the feeling of running in place.
This is really what the reformist approach is all about—the hope that by pushing for better conditions, even within a flawed system, life can get fairer. It’s practical. It’s hopeful. After all, who wouldn’t want to make things better, even if it’s just one step at a time? For most people, the idea of a revolution feels risky, maybe even scary. Why gamble everything, when you can win something today?
But here’s the tricky part. The system itself is pretty good at absorbing change, without ever really changing at its core. Maybe the factory owners complain about new rules, but they adjust. Sometimes, they just pass the extra cost on to their customers. Other times, they cut corners somewhere else. Or they simply wait it out, hoping things will swing back their way. The big picture, the real structure of power, stays the same—the folks who own things, and the folks who work for them.
And over time, you start to see the limits. Reforms matter, sure. They can make life less harsh. But they can’t eliminate exploitation. They can smooth out some edges, but they can’t make the system truly fair. The rules might shift, but the game itself? That keeps going.
This isn’t just theory. It shows up in everyday life. Maybe there’s a new law that makes a workplace safer. That’s great! But does it guarantee a wage you can actually live on? Or maybe the minimum wage goes up, but suddenly, rent does too. Each win is real, but it’s also fragile—always at risk of being rolled back.
When you look closer, the pattern gets hard to ignore. The whole system seems built to protect those at the top. Sure, reforms can blunt some of its sharpest edges, but the core remains unchanged. Inequality isn’t just an accident—it’s baked into how things are organized.
As the workers file out of that hall, some feel proud of what they’ve managed to achieve. Others are frustrated by how little has really changed. Most feel a mix of both. The promise of reform is real—but so are its limits. And that leaves us with a big question: Is it enough to just make things a little better? Or is it time to imagine something more?
